title: Earth’s Falcons Have the Heights to Visit
intro: In 2015 Ihab al-Shabatat posted an earlier version of this poem with the dedication “To the spirit of that young man”. A solitary walker recalls his childhood, carries Baghdad to Sana'a in a dream and sees a bride's hand in the leaves of a grapevine in Tafila. In Khalid al-Sharafi's recording the closing verse is heard twice, as a pain shared by many parts of a body gives way to their power to heal each other.

translation: Earth's falcons have the heights to visit.
Spirits draw close among their peers.
1.sharh: The falcon belongs to the earth and yet is at home high above it. That affinity supplies a way of understanding why certain people, too, draw naturally together.

translation: Life, barren among its people, has done me no harm.
Flowers give birth to nectar in my cup.
2.sharh: The flowers answer the apparent barrenness of human life with a birth of their own. The nectar actually reaches his cup, bringing the answer within his grasp.

translation: Spring's fountains delight in a sip
of poets' blood that takes possession of the mouth.
3.sharh: The springs seem to drink as well as flow. The sip comes from poets' blood and takes over the mouth, the very place from which a poem issues.

translation: Breezes off the flowers' cheeks shade me from within
if some speck's thorn cries out against me.
4.sharh: A flower has a cheek from which a breeze can reach inside him. Against this shelter he sets an enemy with a thorn scarcely larger than a mote and a disproportionately loud voice.

translation: I no longer recognised the ruins where I once knew longing.
I grew fair in my very roots, with no outward sign.
5.sharh: At a ruined dwelling a poet might expect the old love to reveal itself. This speaker barely recognises the place, and the change in his own roots is equally hard to read from the outside.

translation: The verses struck my heart until I thought them
strung together from the shavings of my insides.
6.sharh: A poem can be strung together like beads. Here the poet supplies the material himself, the painful shavings pared from his own body.

translation: I walk alone through the deep darkness of humankind.
My mind casts light on the rest of the living.
7.sharh: The darkness he walks through is a human crowd. His mind sends its light out to the same people whose company has left him feeling alone.

translation: The sleepless wilderness held me through the nights.
I felt my way towards myself, with everyone facing me.
8.sharh: He gives the desert his own insomnia. With everyone in plain view before him, it is his own self that he must seek as someone with poor sight seeks a light at night.

translation: In the scowling night the mountains see
what the ankles of the dusty earth cannot see.
9.sharh: The mountains stand high enough to look out over the dark. Giving the earth ankles brings the opposing point of view almost down to the ground.

translation: People loom large with the weight of their presence.
Their minds are weighed by the views they hold.
10.sharh: People can make themselves loom large. Opinions provide another set of scales on which the mind, as distinct from the imposing figure, can be weighed.

translation: I see the stars of night in their fetters,
and care draws me back towards my ailments.
11.sharh: The stars' fixed places look like shackles. Instead of finding distraction overhead, he sees his own confinement reflected there.

translation: Memories of childhood surge in haste,
and dreams rise up that loathe my losses.
12.sharh: The memories move so violently that childhood seems to break into the present. His dreams themselves recoil from the losses the grown man has suffered.

translation: I see visions whose footsteps are a riddle.
They fly with Baghdad all the way to Sana'a.
13.sharh: At first he looks for the footprints of a dream. Then the dream takes flight, carrying Baghdad itself to Sana'a with a freedom no traveller on foot could have.

translation: Childhood laughter sounds tomorrow, as I repeat
a song that gazes towards my echoes.
14.sharh: Remembered laughter can still lie ahead of him. The song he repeats is given eyes and turns back towards its singer, listening for what will return.

translation: I saw the mouth of the universe smile. In
my hand was a palm shoot from the scent of my dew.
15.sharh: The whole universe can smile, but the sign of life he can touch fits in one hand. He imagines a young palm growing from the fragrance of his own dew.

translation: The scent of date clusters spreads through its reaches,
as I watch for judgement on the enemies.
16.sharh: The palm shoot has grown, in imagination, into scented fruit reaching far beyond his hand. The anticipation of a reckoning with enemies enters even this scene of plenty.

translation: Distant even in her nearness, she is like
the grapes of Tafila in the season of the Twins.
17.sharh: His elusive vision acquires the taste of fruit from a particular place and season. The grapes are near enough to imagine, yet belonging to a season gives them a distance too.

translation: Leaves sway amid their greenery
like a bride's hand on henna night.
18.sharh: A swaying leaf becomes the gesture of a bride holding out her hand for henna. A small movement outdoors calls an entire gathering to mind.

translation: The heavens race around our homes,
and we become something, the very substance of things.
19.sharh: The homes he knows now stand at the centre of the sky's motion. The distance from an ordinary “something” to “the substance of things” is crossed in a single breath.

translation: They cast the seeds of dawn into our wombs,
and the germ of the next frail life sinks deep.
20.sharh: Dawn becomes a crop planted inside people. Beside that promise of light the poet sets another beginning, the seed of someone vulnerable disappearing into the depths.

translation: Souls defend their pools with lips for sipping,
their reeds reaching into murky water.
21.sharh: The souls guard the water on which they live. The reeds leading from where they sip reach something turbid, leaving the precise source of what they drink hard to see.

translation: The earth's flame is plain in our breath.
Why, then, are our ribs tents of winter?
22.sharh: Breathing out gives evidence of an inner fire. Yet the ribs above it look like the poles of a tent sheltering winter itself.

translation: In every breast whose beating heart rose above
the dew's soft shoe on paths of scorching sand,
23.sharh: Dew acquires a foot covering delicate enough to feel out a path over burning ground. The beating breast carries the encounter between coolness and heat on from the winter ribs.

translation: peace spoke its greeting eloquently.
The tongues of wars could only stammer back.
24.sharh: Peace need only say its own name to offer a greeting in Arabic. Wars have many tongues, yet all they can manage in reply is a repeated consonant.

translation: Morning licked our soil, too proud to let
the depths vie over the martyrs they hold.
25.sharh: Morning stoops right down to the soil. In the speaker's image even the depths of graves have no claim to outrank one another by those who lie there.

translation: Its rays were dusted with their blood
as a man is dusted by the gravel.
26.sharh: Light behaves like a body that has lain on the ground. What clings to it in place of dust is blood, bringing the dead into the colour of morning.

translation: Time scattered its sands for our promises.
Our breaths race with them across the sandy waste.
27.sharh: The promises have to keep pace with time as its grains scatter. Breath itself is pictured running through a landscape made of the same material.

translation: A meadow's ears of corn grew thick in its air
with newborn wheat, yellow of cheek.
28.sharh: The meadow fills with ears of corn. Looking closely, he gives the new wheat a child's cheek already coloured with the yellow of ripeness.

translation: The air drank down the clouds' cloak
and cast its threads on the stony ground.
29.sharh: The cloud begins as a whole garment and comes down to earth in thin threads. Their fall gives the rain the appearance of fabric coming apart.

translation: The dragonflies' lovely music sounds over the hills,
courting the brightness of the weather stars.
30.sharh: The wings of insects make music just above the hills. The object of its courtship is much farther off, the gleam of stars by which weather and rain were once reckoned.

translation: The eastern shore gathered up a cloud
orphaned by the exile of those far away.
31.sharh: The shore is able to take a cloud in its arms. Calling the cloud an orphan makes its arrival feel like the end of a long separation.

translation: Any exile may one day grow easy for a young man,
except exile in the company of the ignorant.
32.sharh: Distance from home can ease with time. The difficult exile here is felt while sitting in a gathering, with other people close at hand.

translation: The gate of darkness is closed to footsteps.
Its locks are sealed with blood.
33.sharh: Darkness has become somewhere a walker might try to enter or leave. A gate, several locks and a seal of blood bring the walker's progress to a halt.

translation: The stars of night sing a mocking light
at fears held prisoner in the dark.
34.sharh: Stars now sing in light. Earlier they appeared fettered themselves, while here the prisoners in the dark are thoughts that trouble the speaker.

translation: The pain each part had shared stirred through the whole,
and the limbs healed one another.
35.sharh: Pain travels from the part to the whole body. The same bond allows the limbs to bring healing to one another, the thought on which the reciter dwells a second time.

1.1.3.head: زَورَة
1.1.3.meaning: A visit or a single flight to call on someone.

1.1.4.head: العَلياء
1.1.4.meaning: The heights, with a further sense of eminence or glory.

3.2.1.head: تَقَمَّصَ
3.2.1.meaning: To put something on like a shirt, hence to assume its form or enter into it.

4.2.4.head: هَباءَة
4.2.4.meaning: One mote, like a particle of dust visible in a shaft of light.

5.1.2.head: أَطلال
5.1.2.meaning: The remains of a dwelling after its people have gone.

5.1.5.head: جَوى
5.1.5.meaning: A consuming ache of love or sorrow.

5.2.1.head: هَيُؤَ
5.2.1.meaning: To grow fair in appearance. The poet places the change in his roots.

5.2.4.head: سيماء
5.2.4.meaning: A visible or distinguishing mark, especially in the face.

6.1.1.head: فُئِدَ
6.1.1.meaning: To be stricken in the heart.

6.2.2.head: نُشارَة
6.2.2.meaning: Sawdust or shavings left by the saw, here from the poet's own insides.

8.2.1.head: عَشا
8.2.1.meaning: To feel one's way towards something in the dark, as towards a distant fire.

9.2.4.head: كَواحِل
9.2.4.meaning: Ankles, the joint low on the body, transferred to the earth.

9.2.5.head: الغَبراء
9.2.5.meaning: The dust-coloured one, an old name for the earth.

12.1.1.head: مارَ
12.1.1.meaning: To surge or sway back and forth.

12.2.3.head: قَلى
12.2.3.meaning: To loathe or recoil from. The dreams themselves do so here.

13.1.3.head: أُحجِيَّة
13.1.3.meaning: A riddle whose answer has to be worked out.

13.2.2.head: بَغداد
13.2.2.meaning: Baghdad, capital of Iraq, carried bodily along in the vision.

13.2.4.head: صَنعاء
13.2.4.meaning: Sana'a, the Yemeni city where the dream's flight ends.

14.2.2.head: رَنا
14.2.2.meaning: To gaze steadily, often with longing.

15.1.2.head: ثَغر
15.1.2.meaning: The mouth, especially its opening when someone smiles.

15.2.2.head: فَسيل
15.2.2.meaning: Young date-palm offshoots taken for planting.

16.1.2.head: العُذوق
16.1.2.meaning: Date clusters on their hanging stalks.

16.2.2.head: دَينونَة
16.2.2.meaning: Judgement, a reckoning for what someone has done.

17.2.2.head: الطَّفيلَة
17.2.2.meaning: Tafila, a town in southern Jordan, evoked through its grapes.

17.2.4.head: الجَوزاء
17.2.4.meaning: Al-Jawza', a stellar name also used for Gemini, the Twins. Here it marks a season.

18.2.3-4.head: لَيلَة الحِنّاء
18.2.3-4.meaning: “Henna night” is a wedding celebration at which the bride's hands are dyed with henna.

19.1.2.head: الأَفلاك
19.1.2.meaning: The celestial orbits, pictured as the moving heavens.

20.2.1.head: غارَ
20.2.1.meaning: To sink deep and disappear from sight.

21.1.1.head: مُهَج
21.1.1.meaning: Souls or lives, originally the heart's blood.

21.1.2.head: ذادَ
21.1.2.meaning: To ward off a threat, to defend.

21.1.3.head: حِياض
21.1.3.meaning: Pools or watering places. Guarding them can mean defending one's home.

21.1.4.head: مَراشِف
21.1.4.meaning: Places at which a liquid is sipped, a word also used for lips.

21.2.3.head: الكَدراء
21.2.3.meaning: Dusky or turbid. The surrounding image of pools favours murky water.

23.1.3.head: خافِقَة
23.1.3.meaning: Something in fluttering motion, as a banner in the wind. The mention of a heart gives it a pulse as well.

23.2.1-2.head: خُفّ النَّدى
23.2.1-2.meaning: “The dew's soft shoe” gives it a foot to travel with. The word can also mean a camel's padded foot.

23.2.4.head: الرَّمضاء
23.2.4.meaning: Ground baked hot by the sun.

24.2.1.head: لُسُن
24.2.1.meaning: Tongues, the organs of speech given to wars here.

24.2.4.head: الفَأفاء
24.2.4.meaning: The stammerer's repeated f sound, heard here in war's attempted reply.

25.1.4.head: أَنَف
25.1.4.meaning: Out of proud reluctance or disdain.

27.1.4.head: عِدات
27.1.4.meaning: Promises. The poet's earlier text vowels the first consonant with i.

27.2.5.head: الرَّملاء
27.2.5.meaning: Evokes the sand scattered by time. The word can also describe a lean or rainless year.

28.1.1.head: أَثَّ
28.1.1.meaning: To grow thick or luxuriant, said of vegetation.

28.1.3.head: مَرجَة
28.1.3.meaning: A grassy meadow or stretch of pasture.

28.2.4.head: الوَجناء
28.2.4.meaning: An old epithet of a full-cheeked she-camel. Here it suggests the yellow cheek of the newborn wheat.

29.1.1.meaning: To drink in large continuous gulps.

29.2.5.head: الصَّمّاء
29.2.5.meaning: Hard and unyielding like solid rock.

30.1.2.head: اليَعاسيب
30.1.2.meaning: Dragonflies. The same name also has an older use for a leading bee.

30.2.3.head: الأَنواء
30.2.3.meaning: Stars whose risings and settings were used in Arab weather and rain lore.

31.2.4.head: البُعَداء
31.2.4.meaning: Those far off, here people far from home.

32.1.2.head: اِغتِراب
32.1.2.meaning: Exile or estrangement. The first occurrence can sound like turab, “earth”. Both the poet and the studio give “exile” in both halves.

34.2.3.head: حَبسَة
34.2.3.meaning: Confinement, the condition of being held back or shut in.

35.1.3.head: القَسيم
35.1.3.meaning: What has a share or is shared out. It is set beside the whole in the same phrase.
